name: White button mushroom extract

lead: White button mushroom is an everyday food. Users aiming for a better testosterone-to-estrogen balance include it, or its extracts, among natural aromatase inhibitors, hoping for lower estrogen and a leaner look.

Extracts have been reported to reduce aromatase activity in enzyme assays, with white mushroom showing the greatest effect. A 2009 case-control study in southeast China linked higher mushroom intake to lower breast cancer incidence. Human trials found were registered for cancer-related questions; none addressed appearance.

paras: People eat it as a regular food or take concentrated extract capsules. No appearance timeline is described.

As a common food it is widely eaten; safety data for concentrated extracts were not reviewed in depth. Wild lookalikes such as the death cap are dangerous, which concerns foraging rather than cultivated product.

angle.text: White button mushroom extract is used by people aiming for a better testosterone-to-estrogen balance, via aromatase inhibition seen in lab assays. Human work is cancer-focused, not about looks.

lead: White button mushroom (Agaricus bisporus) is the common cultivated mushroom, grown in more than 70 countries; its brown form is sold as cremini and the mature form as portobello [1]. Extracts of it are discussed as a food-derived aromatase inhibitor, meaning a substance that might reduce conversion of androgens to estrogens [2].

Wikipedia's aromatase inhibitor page reports that mushroom extracts inhibited aromatase in enzyme assays, with white mushroom showing the greatest effect, and cites a 2009 case-control study in southeast China linking higher mushroom intake to lower breast cancer incidence, which it describes as small and limited [2]. Several small human trials have been registered; this article does not report results for them.

paras: Raw white mushrooms provide about 22 kcal per 100 g and are a source of riboflavin, niacin and pantothenic acid; UV exposure raises vitamin D2 content [1]. The species is a model fungus whose genome has been sequenced [3].

In enzyme assays described by Wikipedia, mushroom extracts reduced aromatase activity, white mushroom most strongly [2]. The page notes this is laboratory evidence and that the population study linking mushroom intake to breast cancer incidence was limited in scope [2].

Registered studies on ClinicalTrials.gov include a Phase I trial of white button mushroom extract in postmenopausal breast cancer survivors (16 participants, started 2008) [4], a Phase I trial in men with recurrent prostate cancer (36 participants, started 2009) [5], a trial on inflammation in obese postmenopausal women at high risk of breast cancer (started 2021) [6], and a Phase II trial on PSA in prostate cancer (suspended) [7]. These registrations concern cancer-related outcomes, not appearance, and no results are summarised here. No studies of white button mushroom extract for appearance or bodybuilding goals were found.
